lesson.title: Sorting Into Buckets: Grouping with Dictionaries
lesson.summary: When you need to collect several items under each key instead of just a running number, a dictionary of lists lets you sort data into labeled buckets in a single pass.
lesson.body:
Counting with dictionaries answers "how many" for each key. Grouping with dictionaries answers a related but different question: "which ones" belong to each key. Instead of mapping a key to a running total, you map each key to a list, and every time you see an item that belongs to that key, you append it to the list. The result is a dictionary where every value is itself a list, a natural place to reuse what you know about lists.

The straightforward way to build this is to check whether the key already has a list started, create an empty one if not, and then append. Dictionaries have a method called setdefault that does the check-and-create step for you in one call: groups.setdefault(key, []) returns the list already stored at key if one exists, or creates an empty list, stores it, and returns that, all in one line, so you can immediately call append on whatever it returns.

```python
words = ["apple", "banana", "avocado", "blueberry", "cherry"]
groups = {}
for word in words:
    key = word[0]
    groups.setdefault(key, []).append(word)
print(groups)
```

```
{'a': ['apple', 'avocado'], 'b': ['banana', 'blueberry'], 'c': ['cherry']}
```

Walk through it: when "apple" is processed, key is "a", groups has no "a" yet, so setdefault creates groups["a"] = [] and returns that new empty list, and append("apple") turns it into ['apple']. When "avocado" comes along later, key is "a" again, and this time setdefault finds the existing list and returns it directly, so "avocado" gets appended onto the same list rather than starting a new one. That is the whole trick: setdefault guarantees a list is there before you try to append to it, no matter whether this is the first item for that key or the fifth.

This pattern shows up constantly: grouping students by grade level, grouping transactions by month, grouping log lines by error type. Anywhere you would say "organize these items by some property they share," a dictionary of lists, built with setdefault, is usually the cleanest tool for the job.
